client: I've been really struggling to keep up with everything lately. Between studying for my finals, working my part-time job, and trying to maintain my position on the debate team, I feel like I'm constantly drowning. I'm not sure talking about it will help - it's not like you can add more hours to my day.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy load right now and feeling overwhelmed by all your responsibilities. When you say you're "constantly drowning," I wonder if you've noticed any specific thoughts that come up when you're feeling this pressure?

client: I keep thinking that I should be able to handle all of this better. Everyone else seems to juggle their responsibilities just fine, but I'm always behind. I guess I feel like if I can't keep up, I'm failing somehow. But I don't know how to change that feeling.
therapist: It sounds like you're being quite hard on yourself, comparing your situation to others while feeling stuck in this cycle of self-criticism. What kind of evidence do you have that "everyone else" is handling everything perfectly?

client: Well, I don't know for sure if everyone else is handling things perfectly, but they seem to be. My debate team partner always has their speeches ready, and my coworker at the part-time job never seems stressed. I guess I just assume they're managing better than me because they don't look overwhelmed like I feel.
therapist: It sounds like you're making assumptions about others based on how they appear, while being very aware of your own internal struggles. I notice you're describing this with a sense of thoughtful reflection rather than intense distress right now. What do you think might be different if you approached your situation with the same compassion you're showing as you analyze this?

client: That's an interesting point - I hadn't considered that. I guess if I treated myself with more compassion, maybe I wouldn't feel so panicked all the time. But it's hard because I still feel like there's just too much to do, and being kinder to myself doesn't actually make the workload go away.
therapist: It sounds like you're recognizing the value of self-compassion while still feeling weighed down by practical concerns. Since the workload itself can't change right now, what small adjustments could you make to how you approach these tasks that might help you feel less overwhelmed?

client: I guess I could try breaking things down into smaller steps instead of looking at everything as one huge mountain. But honestly, even thinking about organizing it all feels exhausting. What if I try to make changes and still feel just as overwhelmed? That would just be another failure.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between wanting to try a new approach and fearing that it might not work out, which is completely understandable. Since you're feeling this mix of tiredness and uncertainty, maybe we could start by focusing on just one area - perhaps your studies - and see what small, manageable steps might look like there?

client: I suppose I could try focusing just on my history exam first - that's the one stressing me the most. But even that feels overwhelming because the material is so dense. I'm worried that if I break it into small pieces, I'll lose sight of the big picture and still fail.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two worries - either the material feels too big to tackle all at once, or breaking it down might make you lose track of what's important. Since you're feeling this thoughtful but somewhat stuck right now, what would a helpful balance look like between focusing on smaller pieces while still keeping the overall picture in mind?

client: I guess I could try creating chapter summaries first to keep the big picture in mind, then focus on smaller sections. But I'm worried this will take even more time than my current approach. I always end up feeling like I should be studying every moment I'm not working or at debate practice, which makes any new system seem too slow.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between wanting to try a new approach and feeling trapped by the pressure to use every possible moment for studying. That tension between wanting to change and fearing it might backfire feels very real for you right now. What would help you give yourself permission to experiment with this new approach, even if it feels slower at first?

client: I guess if I could remind myself that my current approach isn't working well either, that might help. But part of me feels like I should just push through the exhaustion because that's what "successful" people do. It's hard to believe that going slower could actually help me get more done in the end.
therapist: It sounds like you're recognizing that your current approach isn't serving you well, yet there's still this powerful belief that pushing through exhaustion is somehow the "right" way. That belief seems to be creating quite a tug-of-war for you. What evidence have you seen, either in your own experience or others', about whether pushing through exhaustion actually leads to better results?

client: Honestly, when I push through exhaustion, I make more careless mistakes and end up having to redo work. I've seen my debate partner take breaks when they're stuck, and they always come back with better arguments. But I still feel guilty when I'm not working - like I'm being lazy even though I know rationally that's not true.
therapist: It sounds like you're starting to recognize that pushing through exhaustion might actually be counterproductive, even though there's still that lingering guilt when you take breaks. You described this with thoughtful awareness rather than intense distress, which suggests you might be ready to gently challenge these beliefs. What do you think might help you start giving yourself permission to take breaks without feeling guilty?

client: Maybe setting a timer could help - like telling myself I'll work for 45 minutes and then take a 15-minute break. But I'm worried I'll just spend the whole break time stressing about what I should be doing instead of actually resting. It feels like my brain won't let me relax even when I try.
therapist: It sounds like you're recognizing the value of structured breaks but still struggling with the guilt that creeps in during those rest periods. Since you're feeling this mix of thoughtful consideration and mild worry, what small experiment could you try to make those breaks feel more genuinely restorative? Perhaps something simple like stepping outside for fresh air during that time?
